why: Visual essays where the data IS the story. Every piece invents its own visual language rather than reusing a chart type.
Proof that a dataset can carry beauty and wit. Colour used as information, never decoration.
Two people hand-drew their data on postcards for a year. THE model for hand-made information design — no software, no chart library, still rigorous.
Typeface choices documented in the wild, by era and industry. Where to go when a page needs a voice we have not used yet.
An argument against the default. Our standing risk is picking the same two families forever.
Letterforms as ornament and event. Useful when a page's whole job is one line.
Numerals as the design. Directly feeds the census page, the tracker, the biblical-numbers system.
Type as a physical object with light behaviour — a reminder that letters can be made, not set.
Scanned design books and manuals. Primary sources for how print actually looked before software.
The ad-parody family (Free Store, Supply Co, mail-order) lives or dies on period accuracy.
Poster thinking: one idea, arm's length, no second chance. The opposite of web reading.
Menus as designed objects — feeds THE TABLE (Isaiah 55) and every listing page.
Layouts so good the reading is secondary. Permission to let a page be an object.
Packaging and shelf design — the visual grammar behind our circular and cereal-box pages.
Where colour is the argument. Antidote to our habit of one palette across an entire issue.
Identity systems with range — the same system producing wildly different artefacts. Exactly our problem.
Marks that outlived their era. Relevant to the BTS wordmark and any department flag.
Title sequences: type, motion and image doing one job together. Great source for section openers.
When the photograph does the work. Feeds the photo essay and the ordinary-places doctrine.
Weather as mood — direct for the Weather desk and the night pages.
Framing and light reference for anything we shoot ourselves.
Portrait reference for real people we profile — never for anyone from the Bible.
Character over polish. A useful corrective to designed-looking people photography.
Studio portraiture conventions — relevant to the yearbook and directory pages.
Vernacular portrait tradition. Warm, odd, real — the opposite of stock.
Community studio photography — the aesthetic of people photographing themselves well.
Shelf density, hand-lettered signage, colour without a system. Real vernacular energy.
Mid-century leisure palettes and travel graphics — a world we have not touched.
Grid, clue typography, answer conventions. Direct for the games block.
Dials, readouts, exposure marks — a mechanical visual language for diagrams and trackers.
Kept deliberately: the thing our PAPER must never look like. Fine for the workspace.
Geometric vocabulary beyond circles and rectangles.
Structural repeat and texture — a way to make a background that is not a gradient.
Cut-out object culture — feeds the wax packs, trading cards and object pages.
The parent library. Where to go when a page needs a world we have not yet borrowed from.
